In summary, our research is concerned with
the plasticity and function of bimodal neurons in the guinea pig dorsal cochlear nucleus.
understanding how multisensory neurons process information from multiple sensory modalities, and how the timing of sensory stimuli can influence the processing of that information.
the role of multisensory processing in the dorsal cochlea nucleus (DCN).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DCN binaural responses are influenced by both stimulus-timing dependent and spike-timing dependent mechanisms.
DCN neurons show Hebbian and anti-Hebbain timing rules that depend upon their intrinsic inhibitory drive.

stimulus-timing dependent synaptic plasticity in the DCN is similar to spike-timing dependent synaptic potentiation and depression at parallel-fiber inputs to DCN principal cells, and is dependent on the inhibitory drive of the DCN neuron.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the timing of multisensory inputs is critical to determine the degree of bimodal plasticity and that the timing rules are influenced by the degree of inhibition.
the DCN is a cerebellar-like structure that uses spike-timing dependent mechanisms to adaptively filter multisensory inputs.

the DCN uses a Hebbian-like mechanism to enhance sound-evoked responses to unexpected somatosensory stimulation, and uses an anti-Hebbain-like mechanism to suppress sound-evoked responses in response to expected somatosensory input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multisensory integration in the DCN is governed by the same plasticity rules that govern synaptic plasticity in the DCN.
the timing rules of plasticity in multisensory circuits are determined by the intrinsic properties of neurons in those circuits, which in turn are determined by the degree of intrinsic inhibition.
multisensory plasticity can be explained by stimulus-timing-dependent plasticity at the level of single synapses.
